title: Map the
current flow
steps.description: We sit with the people doing the work and write down every handoff, tool, and exception. The exceptions are where most automations break.

title: Spec the
workflow
steps.description: We draw the node graph, name the triggers, and agree what happens when a step fails. You approve that before we open n8n.

title: Build and
test
steps.description: We build against your real accounts and real data, then run the workflow in parallel with the manual process and compare the output.

title: Ship and
monitor
steps.description: We cut over, wire failure alerts into a channel your team watches, and hand you the run logs and the documentation.

items.question: Why n8n and not Zapier or Make?
items.answer: n8n can be self-hosted, so your data never leaves infrastructure you control, and it prices per workflow run rather than per task. It also takes arbitrary code in a node, which matters the moment a workflow needs logic a visual builder cannot express.

items.question: What if a tool we use has no integration?
items.answer: If it has an API we can call it directly with an HTTP node and handle the auth ourselves. If it has no API, we look at webhooks, email parsing, or a scheduled export — and if none of those exist, we say so rather than building something fragile.

items.question: Who owns the workflows when the project ends?
items.answer: You do. They run in your n8n instance under your credentials, and you get the exported workflow JSON, the documentation, and a walkthrough. Nothing is locked to us.

items.question: What happens when an automation fails?
items.answer: Every workflow we build has explicit error handling: retries with backoff for transient failures, a dead-letter path for anything that cannot be retried, and an alert into a channel your team already watches. Silent failure is the one outcome we design against.

items.question: How much does an automation cost to run?
items.answer: Self-hosted n8n on a small VPS runs a few dollars a month and covers most workloads. The cost that matters is the API usage of the tools you connect, which we estimate during the spec step before anything gets built.
